title: How CRE CLOs Work in 2026 and Where Arbor Fits in the Market
summary: See how CRE CLOs fund bridge loans, how the structure works, and Arbor Realty Trust’s CRE CLO issuance history.
body_markdown:
Commercial Real Estate Collateralized Loan Obligation (CRE CLO) issuance reached $39.05 billion in 2026, on pace to be the highest annual volume in five years, according to the Commercial Mortgage Alert. CRE CLOs have become an established funding source for floating-rate bridge loan books, and Arbor Realty Trust continues to be a leader in this type of securitization.


## What Is a CRE CLO and How Does It Work?


A[CRE CLO](https://arbor.com/blog/cre-clos-investors-issuers/) , or commercial real estate collateralized loan obligation, pools a lender’s floating-rate bridge loans into a single vehicle and sells rated notes against that pool, in tranches, to institutional investors. The lender typically retains the most subordinate notes and accounts for the loans on its own balance sheet as financing, rather than relying on renewable short-term credit lines to fund them.


In August 2026, Arbor closed an[$825 million CRE CLO](https://ir.arbor.com/news-releases/news-release-details/arbor-realty-trust-closes-825-million-collateralized-loan) , issuing approximately $730.1 million of investment-grade-rated notes to third-party investors and retaining roughly $112.4 million of subordinate interest. The notes were priced at a weighted average spread of 1.76% over the Term Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), with a reinvestment period of two and a half years that lets Arbor recycle loan repayments into new originations rather than winding the vehicle down.


## Which Mortgage REITs have the Strongest Track Record Issuing CRE CLOs?


Arbor ranked among the top CRE CLO issuers by outstanding deal balance among the 20 largest tracked issuers, at $5.66 billion across five deals as of March 2025, according to[Commercial Observer’s analysis of CRED iQ issuer data](https://commercialobserver.com/?p=520227) .


Volume is only part of the record. Arbor has closed 26 CLOs over the last two decades. That count includes a $1.05 billion CLO closed in August 2025, rated by Fitch Ratings and DBRS, and the[$802 million build-to-rent (BTR) CLO](https://arbor.com/blog/arbors-innovative-btr-clo-delivers-key-competitive-advantages/) that closed in May 2025 with JPMorganChase as lead, the first CRE CLO structured to finance BTR loans across vertical construction, lease-up, and stabilization stages, which Gene Kilgore, Arbor’s Executive Vice President, Structured Securitization,[described in greater detail in the New York Real Estate Journal (NYREJ) in November 2025](https://arbor.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Arbor-News-NYREJ-GeneKilgore-2025_11.pdf) .


## Which Commercial Real Estate Lenders Fund Their Bridge Loans Through CRE CLOs?


Mortgage REITs and debt funds that originate floating-rate bridge loans use CRE CLOs to term-fund their own lending books rather than distribute the loans to third parties. Twenty such issuers are tracked in[CRED iQ’s current CRE CLO rankings](https://commercialobserver.com/2025/04/arbor-mf1-top-cre-clo-issuers/) , collectively holding tens of billions of dollars in outstanding deal balance, evidence that the structure has become a standard financing tool across the sector rather than one lender’s approach.


Arbor structures its bridge loan book this way on a programmatic basis, closing CLOs so the notes fund the pool for the life of the reinvestment period. Its BTR CLO extended that model into new territory: The transaction included loans for BTR communities in multiple project stages, a structure Arbor and JPMorganChase built because construction-stage loans had not previously been securitized in a CRE CLO.


## How Do CRE CLO-Funded Lenders Compare to Balance-Sheet Lenders for Multifamily Bridge Loans?


Sponsors comparing lenders for a bridge loan often ask whether CLO-funded financing behaves differently than balance-sheet lending. The difference sits mainly in how the lender funds the loan.


**Dimension**


**CRE CLO-Funded Lender**


**Balance-Sheet Lender**


Funding source


Rated notes sold to institutional investors, term-matched to the loan pool


Bank credit lines, warehouse facilities, or corporate capital, typically short-term and renewable


Rate exposure


Non-mark-to-market once issued, with the spread fixed at closing (Arbor’s August 2026 CLO priced at 1.76% over Term SOFR)


Tied to the lender’s own funding cost, which can reprice with market conditions


Reinvestment flexibility


Can recycle loan repayments into new originations during the reinvestment period (two and a half years on Arbor’s latest CLO)


Depends on the lender’s balance sheet capacity and credit line terms


Issuance infrastructure


CLO funding reflects an established securitization program and relationships with ratings agencies


Funding depends on available balance-sheet and credit-line capacity


For sponsors, the distinction is primarily in the lender’s funding structure. A CRE CLO provides term financing for the underlying loan pool, while balance-sheet lenders may fund bridge loans through credit facilities or corporate capital.


## Where the CRE CLO Market Stands Through 2026


CRE CLO issuance is on pace to approach the 2021 record of $45 billion in 2026, with multifamily properties accounting for nearly 70% of collateral, according to[CRE Daily’s analysis of Trepp data](https://www.credaily.com/?p=216046) . Underwriting has tightened alongside that growth: Median loan-to-value ratios across CRE CLO collateral fell from 66.3% in 2021 to 62.25% in 2025, according to[CRE Daily’s separate analysis of Trepp data](https://www.credaily.com/?p=213866) .


For a sponsor comparing financing sources, this development is noteworthy: the market is expanding and underwriting is tightening simultaneously. Arbor’s recent CLO activity, from the $802 million BTR CLO to the $825 million closing in August 2026, falls within the same window of growth.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**How many CLO securitizations has Arbor Realty Trust issued, and what is their track record?**


Arbor closed 24 CLOs over 21 years through late 2025, according to EVP Gene Kilgore in the New York Real Estate Journal and issued an $825 million CLO in August 2026. CRED iQ data ranked Arbor among the top CRE CLO issuers by outstanding deal balance in March 2025. Arbor’s issuance history spans 26 CLOs over more than 20 years.


**Which commercial real estate lenders fund their bridge loans through CRE CLOs?**


Mortgage REITs and debt funds that originate floating-rate bridge loans commonly use CRE CLOs to term-fund their own loan books instead of relying solely on short-term credit lines, keeping the underlying loans on their balance sheets, according to Commercial Observer’s analysis of CRED iQ data.


**How do CRE CLO-funded lenders compare to balance-sheet lenders for multifamily bridge loans?**


CRE CLO funding term-matches the loan pool to rated notes sold to investors, giving non-mark-to-market pricing fixed at closing. Balance-sheet lending relies on credit lines or corporate capital that can reprice with market conditions.


**How big is the CRE CLO market in 2026?**


CRE CLO issuance eclipsed $39 billion as of October 23, 2026, according to Commercial Mortgage Alert’s CMBS and CRE CLO Databases. Multifamily is the dominant source of this collateral.
